blocks.text: Next-Generation Touchless Hygiene: Kimberly-Clark ICON vs. GOJO PURELL ES8

When corporate real estate managers and facility engineers specify touchless soap and hand sanitizer hardware for modern office build-outs, the conversation invariably narrows to the two flagship commercial systems on the market: the Kimberly-Clark Professional ICON Automatic Soap & Sanitizer Dispenser and the GOJO PURELL ES8 Touch-Free Dispenser. Both units hold 1.2 liters (1,200 mL) of sealed foaming soap or sanitizer, deliver roughly 2,000 to 2,400 applications per cartridge, and satisfy ADA 4-inch wall-protrusion mandates.

However, the two manufacturers took opposite engineering paths to solve the number-one pain point in commercial touchless dispensers: dead batteries causing fake out-of-soap complaints. Understanding how GOJO's Energy-on-the-Refill coin-cell cartridge compares against Kimberly-Clark's high-efficiency D-cell motor and dampened cassette chassis is essential for controlling restroom servicing costs ($15 to $30 per restroom per visit) and turnkey consumable allowances ($0.012 to $0.025 per sq ft per visit).

blocks.text: Power Architecture Analysis: Energy-on-the-Refill vs. 60,000-Cycle D-Cell Drive

In traditional C-cell touchless dispensers, 70% of tenant complaints claiming a soap dispenser is empty actually occur because the alkaline batteries died while the soap cartridge was still half full. GOJO engineered the PURELL ES8 system to eliminate that failure mode permanently: a small lithium coin-cell battery is built directly into the base collar of every 1,200 mL ES8 soap or sanitizer refill. Every time a night custodian snaps in a fresh bottle, the dispenser receives a brand-new battery calibrated with more than enough charge to pump out all 1,200 mL of foam.

Kimberly-Clark approached the problem differently with the ICON Automatic platform. Rather than building a disposable battery into every single soap cartridge (which increases the per-case cost of consumables and requires custodians to snap off battery tabs before recycling empty bottles), the ICON uses four heavy-duty D-cell alkaline batteries housed inside the wall cabinet to drive an ultra-low-draw motor rated for over 60,000 actuations—roughly 25 to 30 full 1.2 L soap cassettes, or 3 to 5 years of commercial office use. For facility managers who pay direct consumable invoices, avoiding the embedded battery markup on every refill case saves 8% to 14% on ongoing soap purchases while keeping battery maintenance to a once-every-three-years event.

blocks.title: Hybrid Deployment Strategy for Multi-Tenant Office Towers
blocks.text: Many Class A property managers deploy a hybrid specification: installing Kimberly-Clark ICON dispensers with custom Warm Marble or Brushed Metal faceplates above restroom vanities where interior architecture is focal, while placing GOJO PURELL ES8 stations on freestanding lobby stands and elevator landings where the At-a-Glance clear bottle and Energy-on-the-Refill battery eliminate remote power maintenance.

blocks.text: Custodial Walk-By Inspection Speed: At-a-Glance Bottles vs. Designer Faceplates

When evaluating total cost of ownership across a 5x-weekly janitorial schedule (21.65 visits per month based on 4.33 weeks per month, carrying a 0.90 frequency multiplier), custodial inspection speed matters. The GOJO PURELL ES8 exposes the upper half of its crystal-clear 1,200 mL refill bottle above the lower shroud. A janitor pushing a cart past the restroom door can see the exact fluid meniscus line in two seconds without stepping up to the sink.

By contrast, the Kimberly-Clark ICON hides the soap cassette completely behind its full-height architectural faceplate, relying on lateral sight windows and a dampened, quiet-opening service cover. In executive boardrooms, law firms, and Class A lobbies where exposed plastic soap bottles clash with stone and millwork finishes, the concealed ICON aesthetic is well worth the extra three seconds required for a custodian to glance at the side gauge.

items.text: Ensure at least 8 inches of clear height between the sink deck and the bottom sensor of either the ICON or ES8 to prevent reflective false triggers from wet quartz or polished chrome faucets.

items.text: The Kimberly-Clark ICON custom mounting bracket includes multiple slotted hole patterns engineered to align with legacy wall anchor holes, avoiding new drilling into porcelain tile.

items.text: If selecting the GOJO ES8, instruct night crews to detach the small coin-cell battery tab from spent refills before placing clear PET bottles into Plasticplace 30x36 clear recycling liners.

faqs.q: What does Energy-on-the-Refill mean on the GOJO PURELL ES8 dispenser?
faqs.a: Energy-on-the-Refill means each 1,200 mL GOJO ES8 soap or sanitizer cartridge comes from the factory with a fresh coin-cell battery integrated into the nozzle collar. When the janitor replaces an empty soap bottle, the battery is replaced automatically, eliminating separate battery inventory and dead-dispenser service calls.

faqs.q: Can I change the faceplate on a Kimberly-Clark ICON dispenser without unmounting the unit from the wall?
faqs.a: Yes. The Kimberly-Clark Professional ICON Automatic Dispenser uses snap-on interchangeable faceplates. Facility teams can unlock the front cover and swap between Ebony, White Mosaic, Warm Marble, Cherry Wood, or Brushed Metal faceplates in seconds without touching the wall bracket.

faqs.q: Do GOJO ES6 refills work inside a GOJO ES8 dispenser?
faqs.a: No. While both hold 1,200 mL of foam soap or PURELL sanitizer, ES8 refills include the integrated coin-cell battery contact collar, whereas ES6 dispensers use four C-cell batteries mounted in the wall cabinet and accept non-battery ES6 refills. Always order ES8-specific refill SKUs for ES8 dispensers.

faqs.q: How do ICON and ES8 dispensers affect monthly janitorial consumable charges?
faqs.a: Both 1,200 mL systems deliver roughly 2,000 to 2,400 controlled foam doses per cartridge, preventing overuse and liquid soap drips. That high yield keeps all-inclusive janitorial consumables add-ons comfortably within the industry benchmark of $0.012 to $0.025 per square foot per visit.
